definition: Focused only on your own small group or place and not interested in outside people or ideas.
example: The village's insular culture made even longtime newcomers feel like permanent strangers.
nuance: Insular stresses being cut off from outside influence, while parochial stresses caring only about local matters.
prompt: A small research lab has rarely shared its work with other teams.
options: The insular lab ignored findings from other universities and kept repeating old methods.
The insular lab eagerly invited visiting scientists from a dozen countries to join every project.
The insular intern rudely talked back to the director during the meeting.
The lab's insular freezer kept the samples cold all through the power outage.
reasons: Shutting out outside work and sticking to familiar habits is exactly what an inward-looking group does.
Welcoming outsiders from many places is the opposite of being closed off.
This confuses the word with insolent; being disrespectful is not the same as being closed off.
This confuses the word with insulated; it describes groups and attitudes, not heat-blocking equipment.

practice.prompt: A high school chess club has played only against its own members for years.
options: The insular club traveled to tournaments across the state just to meet new rivals.
The insular captain mocked the coach to his face and refused to apologize.
The club bought insular mats so the cold gym floor would not chill anyone's feet.
Being so insular, the club had never learned the openings that other schools used.
reasons: Seeking out unfamiliar opponents shows openness, not isolation.
Mocking someone is rude behavior, which mixes up this word with insolent.
Mats that block cold are insulating; this word describes a closed-off mindset, not a material.
Never looking beyond its own members left the club unaware of outside ideas.
